pages.name: In step, then behind
pages.text: These are the turning arrows from Adding waves, drawn at rms. The voltage arrow [[V]], 230 V, points right. The current arrow [[I]], 10 A, starts along it, in step as in a heater, so the power is `230 V × 10 A = 2300 W`. Then I swings 60° behind V, as a motor's current lags. That angle is [[φ]] (phi). Drag I's tip to set it.

pages.name: The in-step part
pages.task: The current is 10 A, 60° behind the voltage. How much of it is in step with the voltage?
pages.why: The in-step part is the floor shadow, the part lying along the voltage arrow: `10 cos 60° = 10 × 0.5 = 5 A`. 8.66 A is the wall shadow, `10 sin 60°`, a quarter turn behind the voltage. 10 A is the whole current, and only part of it is in step.

pages.name: Times 230 V
pages.text: Now multiply every side of that current triangle by the voltage, 230 V. The long side becomes `230 × 10 = 2300` volt-amps (VA), the [[apparent power]]. The flat side becomes `230 × 5 = 1150` watts (W), the [[true power]], which a wattmeter reads. The upright side becomes 1992 VAr (volt-amps reactive), the rate at which energy goes back and forth. The wall shadow carries energy in and back each cycle, so on average it delivers none, as step 9 shows.

pages.name: A motor's power factor
pages.task: A motor on 230 V draws 2.7 A, and a wattmeter reads 450 W. What is its power factor?
pages.why: Apparent power is volts × amps, `230 × 2.7 = 621 VA`. Power factor is true power ÷ apparent power, `450 ÷ 621 = 0.725`. 1.38 divides the wrong way round, and a power factor is never above 1. 621 is the volt-amps themselves, not the ratio.

pages.name: The motor's triangle
pages.text: Here is that motor's power triangle, 621 VA along the long side and 450 W flat. The inverse key gives the angle, `φ = cos⁻¹(450 ÷ 621) = 43.6°`, and Pythagoras gives the upright side, `√(621² − 450²) = 428 VAr`. Put it back to check, `621 × cos 43.6° = 450 W`.

pages.name: From power factor to angle
pages.task: A load has a power factor of 0.5. What is the angle φ between its voltage and current?
pages.why: Power factor is cos φ, so `φ = cos⁻¹ 0.5 = 60°`, with the calculator in degrees. 30° is `sin⁻¹ 0.5`, which takes power factor as sin φ. 1.05 is `cos⁻¹ 0.5` with the calculator in radians mode, the same angle in radians.

pages.name: Hold the true power
pages.text: Now [[Hold true power]] is on, for a 10 kW load on 230 V. In step it needs `10 000 ÷ 230 = 43.5 A`. As φ grows the flat side must stay 10 kW, so the long side stretches to `10 kW ÷ cos φ` and the current bar grows with it. Below, the current is plotted against the power factor.

pages.name: The current at 0.8
pages.task: The same 10 kW load on 230 V runs at a power factor of 0.8 (φ = 36.9°). What current does it draw?
pages.why: The flat side stays 10 kW, so the current is `10 000 ÷ (230 × 0.8) = 54.3 A`, which Electrical A2Z's worked example prints as 54.5 A. A lower power factor needs more current, never less, so `43.5 × 0.8 = 34.8 A` goes the wrong way. 43.5 A is the current at a power factor of 1, so it leaves the power factor out.

pages.name: Where the power goes
pages.text: Holding 10 kW, φ goes on to a power factor of 0.3 (72.5°). The current climbs to 145 A and the curve bends up steeply, because towards 90° the current needed grows without limit. Then Hold true power goes off, the current is back at 10 A, and φ sweeps again from 0° to 90°. Under the triangle is the [[power wave]], volts × amps at each moment, made from the voltage and current waves.
pages.alt: The current, 10 A, lags the 230 V by 90°. Its power triangle has a long side of 2300 VA and a flat side, the true power, of 0 W. Under it the power wave, volts × amps at each moment, averages 0 W.

pages.name: True power at 0.8
pages.task: A load on 230 V draws 10 A at a power factor of 0.8. What is its true power?
pages.why: Apparent power is `230 × 10 = 2300 VA`, and true power is apparent power × power factor, `2300 × 0.8 = 1840 W`, the flat side. 1380 W is `2300 × 0.6`, the upright side. 2875 W divides by 0.8, which would make the flat side longer than the long side.

pages.name: Mixed: two cable runs
pages.task: Two cable runs leave a junction box 60° apart, one 5 m long and one 8 m. How far apart are their ends?
pages.why: Two sides and the angle between them, with no right angle, call for the cosine rule from Triangles without a right angle. `5² + 8² − 2 × 5 × 8 × cos 60° = 25 + 64 − 40 = 49`, so the ends are `√49 = 7 m` apart. 9.43 m is `√89`, Pythagoras, as if the runs were 90° apart. 11.36 m is `√129`, with the minus sign dropped.

pages.name: Mixed: a ship's supply
pages.task: A college's marine notes say 60 Hz is the most common frequency on board ship. How many radians a second does its turning arm sweep?
pages.why: One whole turn is 2π radians, and the arm turns 60 times a second, so it sweeps `2π × 60 = 377` radians a second, the ω of From circle to wave. 60 counts turns, not radians, and 188.5 is `π × 60`, only half a turn each time.

pages.name: Mixed: two currents
pages.task: In a motor circuit two currents join, 4 A in step with the voltage and 3 A a quarter turn behind it. What are the supply current and its power factor?
pages.why: Lay the arrows tip to tail, 4 A along the voltage and then 3 A pointing a quarter turn behind. The supply current is `√(4² + 3²) = 5 A`, and its power factor is the in-step part over the whole, `4 ÷ 5 = 0.8`. 7 A adds the sizes as if both were in step, and 0.6 puts the quarter-turn part on top. Complex numbers, the next course, writes the power triangle's two short sides as one number.
